lesson.subtitle: Lesson 15 -- The Arrival
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 15 -- The Arrival
phases: The Words of the Last Mile

listenings.text: After every final interview I make one call, and I ask the same question: what did you make of him. What comes back is never a summary. It is one sentence, and it is almost always a sentence the candidate said out loud in the room. Sixty days into thirty without losing a client. That is what travels to the people who were not there, and those people vote. So candidates should decide, before the interview, which sentence they want repeated, and then say it slowly, once, in the middle of an answer where it belongs. Not three times, and never in the first minute. The mistake is thinking the panel will summarise you generously. They will summarise you accurately, using your own words.

The interview is not over when you leave the room, and the four hours after it are free points that almost nobody takes. I do three things. I send whatever I promised, the same afternoon, even if it is one page. I write down every question I was asked, in their words, because the next process will ask half of them again. And I write one line about what I would change, which is not the same as what went wrong. Most candidates go home and replay the worst thirty seconds for two days. That is not preparation, it is punishment, and it makes the next interview worse. Send the page, write the questions, choose one thing, and then stop.

extra_audio.text: Claire gives the feedback straight, with the numbers she was given. She says the first sentence is now the strongest part of the answer. She adds the smaller point: three examples where two would have been better. Fernando says where the third example came from, without defending it. He ends by promising the audited page for that afternoon.
